strengths: Practical and well-motivated pipeline combining high-resolution synchronization pre-training, shortcut-augmented flow matching for few-step sampling, and masked training for seamless outpainting.

First successful adoption of shortcut models (Frans et al., 2025) in generative audio / V2A, demonstrating that 8-step sampling achieves comparable quality to 32-step sampling without requiring expensive post-hoc reflow distillation.

Masked flow-matching objective effectively solves the long-form audio generation bottleneck by enabling autoregressive outpainting over short context windows, maintaining stable synchronization and distribution metrics up to 60 seconds (Figure 5).

Strong performance on temporal synchronization: SALSA-V outperforms existing methods (e.g., MMAudio, FoleyCrafter) on both objective DeSync metrics and subjective human evaluation, despite having a smaller parameter footprint (643M vs. 1.03B).

Clear methodology and appendix documentation, including architecture parameters, VAE fine-tuning details, inference classifier-free guidance formulation, and the formal definition of the Sliced-Wasserstein Spectral Distance (SWSD).
weaknesses: The human evaluation is conducted on a relatively small test set of only 10 videos with 18 participants (180 total trials), which limits statistical power and generalizability across diverse video categories.

While synchronization is notably improved, subjective audio quality is lower than MMAudio (MOS of 2.96 vs. 3.16), and objective quality metrics (KLPANNs, IS) show slight degradation; it remains unclear whether this gap is strictly attributable to parameter count differences or architectural trade-offs.

Ablations are limited to model size and shortcut vs. flow-matching loss (Table 2); there are no component-level ablations evaluating the exact impact of the VideoPrism-based synchronization encoder versus prior features (e.g., Synchformer) or the specific feature upsampling design (Eq. 4).
Minor presentation errors: placeholder link on page 2 ('Samples are available at .') was left blank, and page 8 references Figure 5 incorrectly as 'Section 4.1' multiple times.

strengths: Addresses two critical and practical bottlenecks in video-to-audio (V2A) generation: the high sampling latency of diffusion/flow models and the difficulty of generating consistent long-form audio beyond 10 seconds.
Effective integration of shortcut learning into latent flow matching, allowing high-fidelity generation in as few as 8 sampling steps without requiring separate distillation or reflow stages.
The masked flow matching formulation elegantly provides native support for audio-conditioned generation, inpainting, and chunked long-form outpainting, demonstrating robustness up to 60-second clips.

Comprehensive implementation details documented in the appendix, including the custom length unification module, VAE fine-tuning to 43 Hz, and the algorithmic definition of the Sliced-Wasserstein Spectral Distance (SWSD).
weaknesses: One of the three core contributions highlighted in the introduction is the contrastively-trained audio-visual alignment model using VideoPrism; however, there is no ablation isolating the effect of this new module against existing alignment features (e.g., Synchformer) within the proposed generative architecture.

The human evaluation is limited in scale (18 participants evaluating only 10 videos) and lacks error bars, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests. Moreover, the subjective audio quality score is lower than that of MMAudio (2.96 vs. 3.16).
The audio demo link is missing ('Samples are available at .' on page 2), preventing qualitative verification of acoustic artifacts, temporal synchrony, and seamlessness across chunk boundaries.

On standard full-step benchmarks (Table 1), the improvements over the primary baseline (MMAudio) are modest (e.g., DeSync 0.497 vs. 0.521 on a metric with 0.2s temporal resolution; FADVGG 1.07 vs. 1.12).

strengths: SALSA-V introduces an effective, well-engineered architecture that tackles three core pain points in video-to-audio (V2A) generation simultaneously: temporal synchronization, few-step sampling efficiency, and long-form extension.

The incorporation of the shortcut formulation directly into latent flow-matching training avoids cumbersome multi-stage distillation or reflow pipelines. The ablation study in Table 2 demonstrates that shortcut training incurs negligible degradation at higher step counts (32 steps) while maintaining high generation quality and synchronization down to 8 and 4 steps (Figure 5).

The masked flow-matching objective provides a natural mechanism for reference-audio conditioning and outpainting, allowing robust extension to long-form video (up to 60 seconds) without the positional embedding degradation that affects standard full-sequence diffusion models.

Extensive experimental results: SALSA-V outperforms strong baselines like MMAudio and FoleyCrafter on temporal synchronization (achieving lower DeSync and a substantial gain in human MOS synchronization: 3.52 vs. 2.92) while using a significantly smaller parameter footprint (643M vs. 1.03B).

Thorough appendix providing architectural details (e.g., length unification with gated ConvTranspose and stopgrad), training hyper-parameters, VAE fine-tuning details, and a well-formulated Sliced-Wasserstein Spectral Distance (SWSD) metric for evaluating audio conditioning consistency.
weaknesses: The baseline comparisons in Table 1 are somewhat restricted, evaluating only against FoleyCrafter and MMAudio. While MMAudio is a leading recent baseline, quantitative comparisons against other models discussed in the related work (such as Frieren, LoVA, or V-AURA) on standard benchmarks would provide a more complete assessment.

The scale of the human evaluation study is relatively limited, involving 18 participants evaluating only 10 video clips (yielding 180 ratings total). Given the perceptual nature of Foley synthesis and diversity of video genres, a broader sample set would improve confidence in the subjective findings.

As acknowledged in the limitations, progressive outpainting for long-form generation inherently assumes continuity of the acoustic environment and struggle with multi-scene videos containing cuts or abrupt contextual shifts unless manually re-seeded.

The sample repository link is empty ('Samples are available at .'), which deprives reviewers of the ability to qualitatively verify audio fidelity, transient sharpness, and synchronization against video playback.

strengths: SALSA-V effectively tackles multiple key bottlenecks in video-to-audio (V2A) synthesis simultaneously: fine-grained temporal synchronization, high-fidelity few-step inference, and long-form audio generation via iterative outpainting.

The application of shortcut flow-matching (Frans et al., 2025) directly within the base training loop is well-motivated and executed, enabling competitive generation in as few as 4 to 8 steps without requiring multi-stage reflow or distillation.

The synchronization module built on the VideoPrism vision backbone and an Audio Spectrogram Transformer yields noticeable improvements in audiovisual alignment, as shown by lower DeSync scores and higher subjective human ratings for synchronization.

The empirical validation is thorough, spanning standard objective benchmarks (FAD, KL, IS, ImageBind score, DeSync), latency comparisons, step-budget/duration scaling curves, Mel-spectrogram analyses, and a dedicated spectral evaluation metric (SWSD).
weaknesses: While the system as a whole is well-engineered and effective, the core technical components primarily adapt and combine established methodologies (shortcut learning, masked token replacement from VampNet, and contrastive pre-training inspired by Synchformer using VideoPrism).

The human evaluation is somewhat limited in scale (18 participants on 10 video clips) and only benchmarks against two baseline models (MMAudio and FoleyCrafter), leaving out other recent competitive baselines.

In Table 1, the model's subjective quality rating (2.96) is slightly lower than MMAudio (3.16), and its distribution-matching metric KLPANNs (1.81) is behind AudioX (1.70) and MMAudio (1.77), indicating that improved temporal alignment may come with slight trade-offs in perceived fidelity.

The training pipeline relies partially on non-public data ('high-fidelity studio Foley set') and custom pre-filtering thresholds, which presents reproducibility challenges for researchers attempting to reproduce the exact setup.

strengths: Addresses multiple critical bottlenecks in video-to-audio (V2A) synthesis simultaneously: high inference latency, lack of long-form audio generation capability, and temporal misalignment.

The integration of the shortcut model formulation into latent flow matching enables native few-step generation (e.g., down to 4–8 sampling steps) without requiring a multi-stage distillation or reflow pipeline, achieving an inference time of 0.71s for 10-second clips.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation comparing against strong modern baselines (MMAudio, Frieren, LoVA, FoleyCrafter) across standard objective metrics (FAD, KL, DeSync, ImageBind score), scaling behaviors, and sampling efficiency.
The masked flow matching formulation is cleanly utilized both for audio reference conditioning and iterative outpainting for long-form synthesis up to 60 seconds.
Detailed appendix providing architecture specifications, contrastive pretraining details, the proposed Sliced-Wasserstein Spectral Distance (SWSD) algorithm, and user study interface design.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is largely integrative: the system effectively combines existing paradigms—shortcut matching (Frans et al., 2025), masked token inpainting/outpainting (VampNet / Chen et al., 2025), MMDiT backbone, and contrastive alignment (Synchformer approach upgraded with VideoPrism)—rather than proposing a fundamentally new generative formulation.

The human evaluation is limited in scale: it consists of only 18 participants rating 10 videos (180 total trial evaluations across three methods), which provides relatively low statistical power for subtle subjective MOS differences.

The long-form generation mechanism is essentially iterative autoregressive extension using a small sliding context window (0.5s overlap); as acknowledged in the limitations, it is prone to boundary issues and unnatural audio carryover across camera scene cuts.

Evaluation is conducted on a custom aggregated test set (VGGSound test set, UnAV-100, and filtered holdout videos), which complicates direct 1:1 comparison with numbers reported in other published works on standard fixed-length benchmarks.

strengths: Holistic and practical system design addressing three prominent bottlenecks in video-to-audio generation: synchronization accuracy, generation latency (inference steps), and arbitrary-length long-form synthesis.

First application of shortcut models to flow matching in multimodal audio generation, allowing 4-to-8 step sampling without degrading full-step performance or requiring multi-stage distillation / reflowing.
Superior synchronization results demonstrated both objectively (DeSync metric on mixed-length benchmark) and subjectively through a blind human listening study.

Effective masked flow matching paradigm that enables seamless outpainting for long-form audio generation (up to 60s) and reference audio conditioning, supported by clear quantitative metrics (including Sliced-Wasserstein Spectral Distance) and qualitative spectrogram visualizations.

Thorough experimental validation across model sizes (347M, 643M, 1.01B), sampling step budgets, inference runtimes, and sequence durations against strong recent baselines (MMAudio, LoVA, Frieren, FoleyCrafter).
weaknesses: The human evaluation is limited in scale to 10 video clips evaluated by 18 participants; expanding the diversity and number of evaluation clips would provide greater statistical confidence.

Component-level isolation of synchronization performance is somewhat incomplete: it remains unclear how much of the synchronization gain stems specifically from the VideoPrism-based contrastive pretraining versus the upsampled conditioning architecture and MMDiT-X backbone.

Long-form generation relies on iterative chunked outpainting with short prepend contexts (0.5s), which—as noted in the limitations—can struggle across abrupt visual scene transitions or cuts where carrying over acoustic context causes undesirable bleeding.
